physical_harm: The victim suffered swelling marks on her head and left face, ligature marks around her neck, lacerated wounds, and inflamed and congested vagina, leading to her death
number_of_offences: Five counts charged under Sections 364, 376, 377, 302, and 201 IPC; all upheld by courts
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of PW-3, the recovery of various articles made pursuant to the confession of the appellant, the evidence of PW-5 and the report of the Forensic Science Laboratory Ex.A-23 proved beyond all reasonable doubt that it was the appellant alone who after having kidnapped the victim committed unnatural offence as well as rape on her and killed her and thereafter caused disappearance of the evidence of the offences.
witness_credibility: PW-3, the grandmother of the victim, was not an interested witness. Her evidence was not disbelieved despite her age and partial vision, as she could fully see and identify the appellant.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant did not reply when asked about the whereabouts of the victim and ran away. He was apprehended after the victim's body was recovered.
trial_duration: Offence: 19.03.2005; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court: 29.07.2009; Supreme Court: February 23, 2012
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: P.C. Aggarwala, Revathy Raghavan; Counsel for the State: R.K. Gupta, Rajeev Dubey, Kamlendra Mishra
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted and sentenced; High Court: Confirmed conviction and sentences; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, converted death sentence to life imprisonment
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant took away the victim from her house in the presence of her mother and grandmother on the pretext of giving her biscuits, raped and murdered her. The recovery of incriminating items made on the appellant's disclosure statement supported the prosecution case. The post-mortem report and Forensic Science Laboratory report proved beyond all reasonable doubt that the appellant committed the rape and murder.
defence_argument: The defence argued that PW-3, the grandmother of the victim, was an interested witness and her evidence should not be relied on. They also claimed that no Test Identification Parade was conducted, that PW-1 was the only witness to the recovery of articles, and that the weapon used to kill the victim was not recovered, thus lacking proof of the offence under Section 302 IPC.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that a near relative of the victim is not necessarily an interested witness, and that the death sentence should be converted to life imprisonment for a young offender who may reform and is not likely to repeat crimes.
precedent_relied_upon: Rameshbhai Chandubhai Rathod (2) v. State of Gujarat (2011) 2 SCC 764; State of Rajasthan v. Smt. Kalki and another (1981) 2 SCC 752; Myladimmal Surendran and others v. State of Kerala (2010) 11 SCC 129; Takdir Samsuddin Sheikh vs. State of Gujarat and another (2011) 10 SCC 158; Sebastian Alias Chevithiyan v. State of Kerala (2010) 1 SCC 58; State of UP. v. Satish (2005) 3 SCC 114; Bantu v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2008) 11 SCC 113
sentencing_rationale: The Supreme Court converted the death sentence to life imprisonment because the appellant was a young person who may reform and there was no evidence he would repeat crimes. The Court followed the three-Judge Bench judgment in Rameshbhai Chandubhai Rathod (2) v. State of Gujarat.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The appellant was a young person (28 years old) with no prior criminal record, and there was no evidence he would repeat similar crimes in the future. He may reform over time.
other_sentence_order: The life sentence of the appellant is extended to his full life subject to any remission or commutation at the instance of the Government for good and sufficient reasons.
